geo.label: Vietnam and Russia sign the Ninh Thuan 1 agreement (23 March 2026)
geo.text: Vietnam and Russia signed an intergovernmental agreement on 23 March 2026 for Ninh Thuan 1: two VVER-1200 units with 2,400 MW combined at Phuoc Dinh. Vietnam's National Assembly approved the agreement on 24 August 2026. Target: commercial operation between 2030 and 2035.
geo.source: World Nuclear News (23 Mar 2026); NucNet (24 Aug 2026)

geo.label: Thailand-Cambodia clashes (July 2025) and a ceasefire (27 December 2025)
geo.text: Clashes on the Thai-Cambodian border in July 2025 were followed by a ceasefire on 27 December 2025. Carried from the earlier verified Myanmar build; not re-verified in this build.
geo.source: Earlier verified build reference (Myanmar dashboard); not re-verified in this build

geo.label: Myanmar junta's elections (December 2025 to April 2026) and armed-group control
geo.text: The military government held its election in phases from December 2025 to April 2026. Chatham House estimated in January 2026 that armed groups controlled about 38% of the country. Carried from the earlier verified Myanmar build; not re-verified in this build.
geo.source: Earlier verified build reference (Myanmar dashboard); Chatham House (Jan 2026)

arms.label: Ninh Thuan 2: PetroVietnam and KEPCO agree to accelerate talks (9 September 2026)
arms.text: PetroVietnam and Korea Electric Power Corporation agreed on 9 September 2026 to accelerate talks on Ninh Thuan 2. PetroVietnam has acquired almost all the land the plant needs. Japan had withdrawn from the project earlier.
arms.source: Nuclear News Network (Sep 2026); World Nuclear Association (2026)

arms.label: No declared nuclear weapons or weapons storage in South-East Asia
arms.text: No South-East Asian state has declared nuclear weapons or weapons storage. The region is a nuclear-weapon-free zone under the 1995 Bangkok Treaty, which entered into force in 1997 (public information). Nuclear material in the region is research-reactor fuel, for example at Dalat, which uses Russian-supplied fuel.
arms.source: Bangkok Treaty text (public information); World Nuclear News (Mar 2026)

arms.label: No operating nuclear power plant in South-East Asia
arms.text: No nuclear power plant is operating in South-East Asia. The WRI database used here lists only the two Chinese plants on the Hainan and Guangxi coast inside this frame. The Philippines' Bataan plant was completed but never operated (public information; not verified in this build).
arms.source: WRI Global Power Plant Database (2018 data, CC-BY 4.0); public information

arms.label: First BrahMos coastal battery in service with the Philippine Marine Corps
arms.text: The first BrahMos battery was shown in November 2025 during the Marine Corps' 75th anniversary and is based in Western Luzon. Each battery has two launchers, a radar vehicle and a reload vehicle. Reports say a further base is planned in northern Luzon and that the programme will reach three batteries.
arms.source: Janes (Nov 2025); USNI News (Jul 2026); Naval News (Mar and Oct 2026)

milops.label: Philippines: nine EDCA sites; the government says they remain Philippine installations (2 March 2026)
milops.text: The Department of National Defense said on 2 March 2026 that the EDCA sites are Philippine facilities, not US bases, and are not used to launch or stage attacks. The nine sites are Basa, Fort Magsaysay, Lumbia, Antonio Bautista, Mactan-Benito Ebuen, Naval Base Camilo Osias, Camp Melchor dela Cruz, Balabac and Lal-lo. A Senate committee chair called for a review amid concern about Iranian attacks.
milops.source: Philstar (2-3 Mar 2026); Manila Bulletin (2 Mar 2026); Tribune (1 Mar 2026)

milops.label: Balikatan 2026 held in northern Luzon, Palawan and the Batanes Islands
milops.text: The US-Philippines Balikatan 2026 exercise took place in northern Luzon, Palawan, the Batanes Islands and other areas of the Philippines (SCSPI report).
milops.source: SCSPI, US military base expansion report (2026)

naval.label: Indonesia cuts first steel for its first Scorpene Evolved submarine (7 August 2026)
naval.text: PT PAL began building the first of two Scorpene Evolved submarines at Surabaya on 7 August 2026, with Naval Group providing design support. The Navy expects delivery in 2032-33 and says the boats will be operated and maintained in Indonesia.

naval.label: Vietnam's six Kilo-class submarines are based at Cam Ranh Bay
naval.text: The Russian-built Kilo-class boats HQ-182 Ha Noi to HQ-187 Ba Ria-Vung Tau serve with the 189th Submarine Brigade at Cam Ranh Bay. Vietnam completed commissioning of all six by early 2017 (Tuoi Tre News, archived; VietnamPlus).
naval.source: VietnamPlus; Wikipedia (Submarine force, Vietnam People's Navy)

naval.label: Singapore's third Invincible-class submarine arrives at Changi (10 April 2026)
naval.text: RSS Illustrious arrived at Changi Naval Base on 10 April 2026 (MINDEF). RSS Invincible and RSS Impeccable were commissioned on 24 September 2024. Four Type 218SG boats are planned, and two more were ordered in May 2025.

naval.label: Thailand has no submarine in service; the S26T programme resumed in August 2025
naval.text: The Chinese-built S26T programme was amended in August 2025 to use Chinese CHD620 engines, which let construction resume. Sources differ on the first delivery (2027 or late 2028). As of September 2026 Thailand had no submarine in service (Global Military).
naval.source: Global Military (Sep 2026); Wikipedia (List of equipment of the Royal Thai Navy)

naval.label: Malaysia: two Scorpene submarines at Sepanggar; RMN Fleet HQ at Lumut
naval.text: Global Military (2026) lists two Scorpene-class submarines based at Sepanggar, Sabah, and the Fleet headquarters (KD Malaya) at Lumut, Perak. The 15-to-5 modernisation plan consolidates the fleet into five standard classes.

naval.label: East Yulin naval base hosts China's only ballistic-missile submarine base (2024)
naval.text: East Yulin Naval Base on Hainan houses China's only ballistic-missile submarine base. A submarine is shown entering a cave there in satellite imagery (Washington Post, 2024).

us_base.label: USS Cincinnati visits China-funded Ream Naval Base (January 2026)
us_base.text: The USS Cincinnati visited Ream Naval Base on 24 January 2026, the first US warship visit to the Chinese-built port. Cambodia says Ream is open to all navies. US officials and analysts have raised concerns about Chinese access.
us_base.source: Defense News (6 Feb 2026); RFA (2024); AMTI / CSIS

scs.label: China's militarised reefs and the Antelope Reef build (2022-2026)
scs.text: Mischief, Subi and Fiery Cross reefs carry airstrips, radar, hangars, gun and missile emplacements and harbours (CSIS / AMTI; RFA, 2022; Newsweek, 2024). Reuters reported in August 2026 that the first construction phase at Antelope Reef in the Paracels was complete.

scs.label: The 2016 arbitral award on the South China Sea, rejected by China
scs.text: The Permanent Court of Arbitration's 2016 award found China's historic-rights claim to the South China Sea without legal effect. China does not accept the award (public information).
scs.source: Permanent Court of Arbitration (12 Jul 2016; public information)

space.label: Wenchang Space Launch Site on Hainan's coast
space.text: Wenchang is one of China's main launch sites and lies on Hainan's coast, the South China Sea side of the island (Washington Post, 2024). Indonesia's Biak spaceport: not verified in this build.

cyber.label: Myanmar raids KK Park (October 2025); 635 buildings demolished by January 2026
cyber.text: The Myanmar military raided KK Park (Myawaddy) in October 2025. The junta reported 635 illegal buildings demolished by January 2026. C4ADS found new construction, expansion or renovation at 14 of 21 suspected sites in Myawaddy since January 2026.

darkweb.label: US sanctions on scam networks in Shwe Kokko and Sihanoukville (2025)
darkweb.text: The US Treasury sanctioned nine targets in Shwe Kokko, a hub protected by the Karen National Army, and ten in Cambodia, including T C Capital, which owns the Golden Sun Sky Casino complex. Virtual-currency scams and forced labour are cited.

air.label: Indonesian Air Force bases: Halim (command), Iswahjudi (fighters), Sultan Hasanuddin (Su-30s)
air.text: The National Air Operations Command is at Halim Perdanakusuma, Jakarta. Iswahjudi in East Java hosts the 32nd Air Wing (fighters). Sultan Hasanuddin at Makassar hosts the 33rd Air Wing (Su-27 and Su-30). A Su-30MK2 overran the runway at Sultan Hasanuddin on 24 August 2026.

social.label: Thailand cuts power to scam-hosting border towns (February 2025)
social.text: Thailand cut electricity and internet links to scam-hosting towns on the Myanmar border in February 2025 (carried from the earlier verified Myanmar build; not re-verified in this build).
social.source: Earlier verified build reference (Myanmar dashboard); not re-verified in this build

wellbeing.label: World Happiness Report 2026: ranks for South-East Asia not verified in this build
wellbeing.text: The annual report ranks countries for wellbeing. The ranks for these eleven states were not verified in this build; check the report directly.
wellbeing.source: World Happiness Report (annual); not verified in this build

markers.name: Naypyidaw (capital, Myanmar)
markers.note: Capital of Myanmar; seat of the military government since 2005.

markers.name: Bangkok (capital, Thailand)
markers.note: Capital of Thailand.

markers.name: Phnom Penh (capital, Cambodia)
markers.note: Capital of Cambodia.

markers.name: Vientiane (capital, Laos)
markers.note: Capital of Laos. Laos is landlocked and has no navy.

markers.name: Hanoi (capital, Vietnam)
markers.note: Capital of Vietnam.

markers.name: Kuala Lumpur (capital, Malaysia)
markers.note: Capital of Malaysia; the administrative capital is Putrajaya.

markers.name: Singapore (city-state)
markers.note: City-state at the southern end of the Malacca Strait.

markers.name: Jakarta (capital, Indonesia)
markers.note: Capital of Indonesia.

markers.name: Manila (capital, Philippines)
markers.note: Capital of the Philippines.

markers.name: Bandar Seri Begawan (capital, Brunei)
markers.note: Capital of Brunei.

markers.name: Dili (capital, Timor-Leste)
markers.note: Capital of Timor-Leste (East Timor).

markers.name: Mandalay (second city, Myanmar)
markers.note: Second city and former royal capital of Myanmar.

markers.name: Taunggyi (capital of Shan State, Myanmar)
markers.note: Capital of Shan State.

markers.name: Mawlamyine (capital of Mon State, Myanmar)
markers.note: Capital of Mon State, on the Gulf of Martaban.

markers.name: Yangon (Myanmar's main commercial port)
markers.note: Myanmar's largest city and main commercial port.

markers.name: Antonio Bautista Air Base (Puerto Princesa, Palawan): EDCA site
markers.note: One of nine EDCA sites: US forces may rotate here under the 2014 agreement; the government says the sites remain Philippine installations. Near the West Philippine Sea. Position approximate.
markers.source: DND / AFP (2 Mar 2026, via Philstar); Inquirer; SCSPI (2026)

markers.name: Basa Air Base (Pampanga): EDCA site, first EDCA project
markers.note: First EDCA project (a multi-purpose warehouse) was launched in 2023. Runway and facility works were reported as due for completion in 2026 (SCSPI). Position approximate.

markers.name: Fort Magsaysay (Nueva Ecija): EDCA site and training base
markers.note: EDCA site since 2016; described by analysts as the largest training base. Position approximate.

markers.name: Lumbia Air Base (Cagayan de Oro, Mindanao): EDCA site
markers.note: EDCA site since 2016. Position approximate.

markers.name: Mactan-Benito Ebuen Air Base (Cebu): EDCA site
markers.note: EDCA site since 2016. A fuel-storage facility was inaugurated here (SCSPI, 2026).

markers.name: Naval Base Camilo Osias (Santa Ana, Cagayan): EDCA site
markers.note: Added to the EDCA list under the Marcos administration (DND, 2026). Position approximate.

markers.name: Camp Melchor dela Cruz (Gamu, Isabela): EDCA site
markers.note: Added to the EDCA list under the Marcos administration. Position approximate.

markers.name: Balabac Island (Palawan): EDCA site
markers.note: Added to the EDCA list. Analysts say it controls the passage between the South China Sea and the Sulu Sea. Position approximate.
markers.source: Manila Bulletin (2 Mar 2026); Modern Diplomacy (Mar 2026, analysis)

markers.name: Lal-lo Airport (Cagayan): EDCA site
markers.note: Added to the EDCA list. Analysts describe it as close to Taiwan. Position approximate.
markers.source: Manila Bulletin (2 Mar 2026); Modern Diplomacy (Mar 2026, analysis)

markers.name: Subic Bay (Zambales): former US naval base, now a freeport
markers.note: Returned by the US in 1992; now the Subic Bay Freeport Zone. The SCSPI report (2026) says EDCA facilities there must sit inside the Freeport Zone. Analysts report planned ammunition production here; the government has not confirmed it.
markers.source: SCSPI (2026); Modern Diplomacy (Mar 2026, analysis); public information (1992 handover)

markers.name: Batanes Forward Operating Base (Philippines): closest Philippine territory to Taiwan
markers.note: Analysts report that a forward operating base opened in Batanes in 2025. Not verified against an official source in this build.

markers.name: Bataan Nuclear Power Plant (Morong, Bataan): completed, never operated
markers.note: Built in the 1980s but never operated (public information). Not verified in this build; the WRI database does not list it.
markers.source: public information (not verified in this build)

markers.name: BrahMos coastal battery, Western Luzon (Zambales): Philippine Marine Corps Coastal Defense Regiment
markers.note: First battery in service. Each battery has two launchers, a radar vehicle and a reload vehicle; the 290 km supersonic anti-ship missile reaches Scarborough Shoal (Janes; Naval News; USNI News; TurDef). Position approximate.
markers.source: Janes (Nov 2025); Naval News (Oct 2026); USNI News (Jul 2026); TurDef (2025)

markers.name: Planned BrahMos base, northwest tip of Luzon (Coastal Defense Regiment, 273rd Marine Company)
markers.note: Planned to cover the Luzon Strait; Naval News (Mar 2026) reports it from social-media posts. The AFP has not confirmed it. Position approximate.

markers.name: Ninh Thuan 1 (planned): two VVER-1200 units (2,400 MW), Russian intergovernmental agreement (Mar 2026)
markers.note: Phuoc Dinh commune, Thuan Nam district. The intergovernmental agreement with Russia was signed on 23 Mar 2026 (Rosatom; WNN). Vietnam's National Assembly approved the agreement on 24 Aug 2026 (NucNet). Target: commercial operation 2030-2035. Position approximate.
markers.source: World Nuclear News (23 Mar 2026); NucNet (24 Aug 2026); Sputnik (9 Sep 2026)

markers.name: Ninh Thuan 2 (planned): Vinh Hai commune; Korean talks accelerated (Sep 2026)
markers.note: Japan withdrew from this project (reports date the withdrawal to Dec 2025 or Jan 2026). On 9 Sep 2026 PetroVietnam and KEPCO agreed to accelerate talks; PetroVietnam has acquired almost all the land (Nuclear News Network). Position approximate.
markers.source: Nuclear News Network (Sep 2026); World Nuclear Association (2026)

markers.name: Dalat Nuclear Research Reactor (Vietnam): 500 kW research reactor, Russian-supplied fuel
markers.note: Operating since March 1984 at a nominal 500 kW. Its Russian-supplied fuel is used to produce medical isotopes (WNA; WNN, Mar 2026). Position approximate (city).
markers.source: World Nuclear Association (2026); World Nuclear News (Mar 2026)

markers.name: Cam Ranh Bay: Vietnam People's Navy submarine base (189th Submarine Brigade; six Kilo-class boats)
markers.note: Home of the 189th Submarine Brigade (formed 2013) and the six Russian Kilo-class submarines HQ-182 Ha Noi to HQ-187 Ba Ria-Vung Tau. A submarine training centre is here (VietnamPlus; Wikipedia). The 196th Submarine-Commando Brigade is also reported here (Wikipedia). Position approximate.
markers.source: VietnamPlus (submarine brigade); Wikipedia (Submarine force, Vietnam People's Navy)

markers.name: X52 Shipyard, Cam Ranh: navy repair and maintenance of the Kilo submarines
markers.note: Navy-owned maintenance, repair and overhaul shipyard that supports the six Kilo-class boats (Indo-Pacific GeoMill, 2018; older source). Position approximate.

markers.name: Surabaya (East Java): Indonesian Navy 2nd Fleet and submarine base
markers.note: Home port of the Type 209 boats KRI Nagapasa, KRI Ardadedali and KRI Alugoro; the 2nd Fleet Command is based here (Wikipedia). Position approximate.

markers.name: PT PAL Indonesia shipyard (Surabaya): builds two Scorpene Evolved submarines
markers.note: State shipbuilder. First steel was cut on 7 Aug 2026 for the lead Scorpene Evolved boat; the Navy expects delivery in 2032-33 (Antara; Navy Leaders). Naval Group provides design support. Position approximate.

markers.name: Halim Perdanakusuma Air Force Base (Jakarta): National Air Operations Command
markers.note: National Air Operations Command (Koopsudnas) is headquartered here. The base hosts transport and VIP squadrons; the civil airport shares the runway (Global Military, Aug 2026; Wikipedia).
markers.source: Global Military (Aug 2026); Wikipedia (Halim Perdanakusuma International Airport)

markers.name: Iswahjudi Air Force Base (Maospati, East Java): fighter base, 32nd Air Wing
markers.note: Home to the 32nd Air Wing and four other units (ICAO WARI; Global Military, Aug 2026).

markers.name: Sultan Hasanuddin Air Force Base (Makassar): 33rd Air Wing, Su-27/Su-30
markers.note: Su-30MK2 overran the runway on 24 Aug 2026 during a simulated take-off after a major overhaul; the crew was unhurt (migflug, 2026). Position approximate.

markers.name: Manuhua Air Force Base (Biak, Papua): 13th Air Wing; 27th Air Squadron (CN235)
markers.note: ICAO WABB; runway 11/29, 3,571 m (migflug, 2026; Wikipedia). Position approximate.

markers.name: Raden Sadjad Air Force Base (Ranai, Natuna Islands)
markers.note: ICAO WIDO; runway 18/36, 2,560 m (Wikipedia, Indonesian Air Force listing). The Natuna Islands face the South China Sea. Position approximate.

markers.name: Roesmin Nurjadin Air Force Base (Pekanbaru, Sumatra): fighter base
markers.note: Fighter base on Sumatra (Wikipedia, Indonesian Air Force listing). Position approximate.

markers.name: Sabang (Weh Island, Indonesia): northwestern tip of Sumatra
markers.note: Northwestern tip of Sumatra, at the Andaman Sea entrance to the Malacca Strait (public information).

markers.name: Teluk Sepanggar (Sabah): Royal Malaysian Navy's principal submarine base
markers.note: Two Scorpene boats (KD Tunku Abdul Rahman and KD Tun Abdul Razak, commissioned 2009) are based here. A Submarine Training Centre and shore-support infrastructure are here (NTI, 2020; Global Military, 2026).

markers.name: Lumut (Perak): Royal Malaysian Navy Fleet HQ (KD Malaya) and Western Fleet
markers.note: Fleet HQ and Western Fleet headquarters; the RMN's naval air unit is based here (Global Military, 2026; Wikipedia). Position approximate.

markers.name: Lumut Naval Shipyard (Malaysia): domestic construction of RMN ships
markers.note: Builds RMN ships domestically (Global Military, 2026). The Boustead DCNS Naval Corporation refitted the Scorpenes (NTI, 2020).

markers.name: Kota Kinabalu (Sabah): RMN Eastern Fleet (third-party listing)
markers.note: Eastern Fleet headquarters according to a 2026 third-party listing; not confirmed against an official source.

markers.name: Changi Naval Base (Singapore): RSN submarine base (RSS Singapura)
markers.note: RSS Invincible and RSS Impeccable (Invincible class) were commissioned here on 24 Sep 2024; RSS Illustrious arrived on 10 Apr 2026. The Archer-class submarines are also based here (MINDEF; Naval News; Wikipedia). Position approximate.
markers.source: MINDEF (10 Apr 2026); Naval News (Apr 2026); Wikipedia (Invincible-class submarine)

markers.name: Sattahip (Chonburi): Royal Thai Navy Fleet headquarters and Marine Corps HQ
markers.note: Fleet headquarters and Royal Thai Marine Corps HQ (Global Security; Global Military, 2026). The helicopter carrier HTMS Chakri Naruebet is in the fleet (Global Military, 2026).
markers.source: Global Security (Royal Thai Navy bases); Global Military (2026)

markers.name: Mahidol Adulyadej Naval Dockyard (Chuk Samet, Sattahip): RTN shipyard; planned submarine home
markers.note: Royal Thai Navy shipyard; plans exist to base a submarine here (Wikipedia). The Chinese-built S26T programme resumed in Aug 2025 after a contract amendment to Chinese engines; no submarine is in service yet (Global Military, Sep 2026).
markers.source: Wikipedia (Mahidol Adulyadej Naval Dockyard); Global Military (Sep 2026)

markers.name: Ream Naval Base (Sihanoukville, Cambodia): Royal Cambodian Navy base with a Chinese-funded upgrade
markers.note: Reopened after renovation on 5 Apr 2025 (Global Military). CSIS says about half of the port is for Cambodian and Chinese use. US officials alleged PLAN exclusive access to about one-third for up to 30 years (2019); Cambodia denies it. USS Cincinnati visited on 24 Jan 2026 (Defense News). Position approximate.
markers.source: Global Military (2026); Defense News (6 Feb 2026); AMTI / CSIS

markers.name: East Yulin Naval Base (Sanya, Hainan): China's only ballistic-missile submarine base
markers.note: Houses China's only ballistic-missile submarine base; a submarine enters through a cave here (Washington Post, 2024).
markers.source: Washington Post (2024); FAS / USNI News (China v6 build)

markers.name: Zhanjiang Naval Base (Guangdong): PLA Navy fleet headquarters
markers.note: Fleet headquarters (Global Military, 2026, third-party listing; background in the China v6 build).
markers.source: Global Military (2026, third-party); China v6 build (background)

markers.name: Southern Theatre Command (Guangzhou): PLA command for the South China Sea
markers.note: Southern Theatre Command headquarters (background from the China v6 build).

markers.name: Wenchang Space Launch Site (Hainan): China's coastal launch centre
markers.note: One of China's main launch sites, on Hainan's coast (Washington Post, 2024; China v6 build; CNSA / Xinhua).
markers.source: Washington Post (2024); China v6 build (CNSA / Xinhua)

markers.name: Scarborough Shoal: disputed by China, the Philippines and Taiwan
markers.note: Chinese coast guard and Philippine vessels have repeatedly clashed here (press reporting). Position approximate.

markers.name: Spratly Islands: China, Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia, Brunei and Taiwan claim parts
markers.note: China has militarised its seven main features in the Spratlys (AMTI / CSIS; China v6 build). Other claimants occupy their own features.

markers.name: Paracel Islands: occupied by China; claimed by Vietnam and Taiwan
markers.note: China holds the islands; its outposts include radar sites (Geopolitical Futures; ABC, 2025).
markers.source: AMTI / CSIS (China v6 build); Geopolitical Futures; ABC (Jul 2025)

markers.name: Mischief Reef (Spratlys): China-occupied and militarised
markers.note: China began occupying it in 1994 (Newsweek). It has hangars, radar, missile shelters and an airstrip (CSIS analysis; ABC, Jul 2025; RFA, 2022). Also called Meiji Reef (China) and Panganiban Reef (Philippines). Position approximate.

markers.name: Subi Reef (Spratlys): China-occupied and militarised
markers.note: Airstrips, radar domes, missile systems and a deepwater port (Newsweek). The US Indo-Pacific Command said by 2022 that its military infrastructure appeared complete. Position approximate.

markers.name: Fiery Cross Reef (Spratlys): China-occupied and militarised
markers.note: Operational airfield, hangars and radomes; a harbour for China's largest naval vessels (RFA, 2022; Geopolitical Futures). Position approximate.

markers.name: Antelope Reef (Paracels): new Chinese artificial island under construction
markers.note: Reuters reported that the first construction phase was completed (Aug 2026). Reports describe a deepwater port, a quay and the start of a runway (Yahoo News, 21 Aug 2026). Position approximate.
markers.source: Reuters (Aug 2026, via chinaglobalsouth); Yahoo News (21 Aug 2026)

markers.name: Itu Aba (Taiping Island, Spratlys): administered by Taiwan
markers.note: Administered by Taiwan (public information). Not verified in this build.
markers.source: public information (not verified in this build)

markers.name: Second Thomas Shoal (Ayungin): BRP Sierra Madre
markers.note: Philippine-occupied shoal with a grounded naval vessel; resupply disputes have been reported (public information). Not verified in this build.
markers.source: public information (not verified in this build)

markers.name: Thai-Cambodian border (Preah Vihear area): clashes in July 2025; ceasefire 27 Dec 2025
markers.note: Reported clash area. The ceasefire of 27 Dec 2025 is carried from the earlier verified Myanmar build; not re-verified in this build. Position approximate.
markers.source: Earlier verified build reference (Myanmar dashboard); not re-verified in this build

markers.name: Defence Services (Tatmadaw) headquarters, Naypyidaw
markers.note: Seat of the military government. The military seized power on 1 February 2021. Position approximate.

markers.name: Mingaladon Air Base (Yangon): Myanmar Air Force base
markers.note: Myanmar Air Force base beside Yangon International Airport (public information). Position approximate.

markers.name: Sittwe (Rakhine State): Arakan Army contests much of the state
markers.note: Rakhine State capital. The Arakan Army contests control of much of the state (press reporting). Front lines change.

markers.name: Myitkyina (Kachin State): fighting reported around the city
markers.note: Kachin State capital. Fighting between the Kachin Independence Army and the military has been reported around the city (press reporting).

markers.name: Laiza (Kachin Independence Army headquarters, China border)
markers.note: Headquarters of the Kachin Independence Army, on the China border (press reporting). Position approximate.

markers.name: Lashio (northern Shan State): control changed hands in 2024 and 2025
markers.note: Northern Shan State town. Control changed hands in 2024 and 2025 (press reporting). Position approximate.

markers.name: Myawaddy (Thai-Myanmar border): border town with scam compounds
markers.note: Border town where scam compounds have been reported (press reporting). Thailand cut power to border towns hosting such operations in February 2025.
markers.source: press reporting; Thai government (Feb 2025, earlier build)

markers.name: Coco Islands (Myanmar): reported Chinese listening facilities (not officially confirmed)
markers.note: Reports of Chinese electronic listening facilities on these islands are press-reported and not officially confirmed by Myanmar or China.

markers.name: Kyaukphyu deep-sea port and China-Myanmar pipeline terminus (Rakhine)
markers.note: China-backed deep-sea port in Rakhine State, reported as the terminus of the China-Myanmar oil and gas pipelines. Status and terms are reported, not verified.

markers.name: China-Myanmar gas pipeline, Muse crossing
markers.note: Gas pipeline route from the China border at Muse towards Mandalay and Yangon (press reporting). Position approximate.

markers.name: China-Myanmar oil and gas pipeline (Yunnan border route)
markers.note: Pipeline corridor from Yunnan through northern Myanmar (background; China v6 build).

markers.name: Thilawa port and special economic zone (south of Yangon)
markers.note: Port and special economic zone south of Yangon (public information). Position approximate.

markers.name: Dawei deep-sea port project (Andaman coast): status not verified
markers.note: Deep-sea port and industrial zone project on the Andaman coast, announced with Thai backing (press reporting). Status not verified.

markers.name: Coco Channel: strait between the Coco Islands and the Andaman Sea approaches
markers.note: Channel near the Coco Islands, cited in strategic reporting. Position approximate.

markers.name: KK Park (Myawaddy, Kayin State): scam compound raided in October 2025
markers.note: Raided in October 2025; the junta reported 635 illegal buildings demolished by January 2026. C4ADS found new construction, expansion or renovation at 14 of 21 suspected sites in Myawaddy since January 2026. Position approximate.

markers.name: Shwe Kokko (Kayin State): scam hub under the Karen National Army; US sanctions
markers.note: Headquarters of the Karen National Army, per OFAC. OFAC sanctioned nine targets here, including Yatai New City (2025). A planned 120 km2 zone valued at US$15bn (Mekong Eye, Nov 2025). Position approximate.

markers.name: Yulong Bay Park (Myawaddy): scam compound (reported)
markers.note: Reported scam compound a few kilometres from the official Thai checkpoint at Myawaddy (Mekong Eye, Nov 2025). Position approximate (Myawaddy township).

markers.name: T C Capital and Golden Sun Sky Casino (Sihanoukville, Cambodia): scam complex (OFAC designated)
markers.note: OFAC designated T C Capital, which owns the Golden Sun Sky Casino and Hotel, from which virtual-currency scams were run (US Treasury, 2025). Position approximate.

markers.name: Strait of Malacca: one of the world's busiest shipping lanes
markers.note: The EIA describes it as critical for energy bound for China (EIA; SL-ML-IOR build).

markers.name: Singapore Strait: southern exit of the Malacca Strait
markers.note: Southern exit of the Malacca Strait (EIA; SL-ML-IOR build).

markers.name: Sunda Strait (Java-Sumatra)
markers.note: Strait between Java and Sumatra (public information). Not verified in this build.
markers.source: public information (not verified in this build)

markers.name: Lombok Strait (Bali-Lombok)
